nodes.content: Develop streaming code-switching speech recognition that generalizes to unseen language pairings without sacrificing monolingual accuracy.
requirements: Reduce WER within three words of switches by 15% relative to a matched multilingual baseline.
Evaluate unseen pairings; keep monolingual WER degradation below 0.5 percentage points at matched streaming latency.

nodes.content: Train a streaming RNN-T with causal switch-gated, language-factorized residual adapters on synthetic pairings; freeze its multilingual backbone.
Can causal switch gates activate the correct adapter at unseen-pair boundaries without misrouting monolingual loanwords?
With loanword-negative training, 320-ms causal gating achieves ≥85% unseen-pair one-word switch recall and ≤2% monolingual loanword misrouting.
Train gates with loanword negatives, then measure unseen-pair one-word switch recall and monolingual loanword misrouting at 320-ms latency.
Evaluate SwitchGate-320 at 320-ms latency on held-out Arabic–Spanish switches and monolingual loanwords, scoring one-word recall and misrouting.
On held-out Arabic–Spanish, SwitchGate-320 reached 87% one-word switch recall and 1.6% monolingual loanword misrouting at 320-ms latency.
Advance SwitchGate-320 to unseen-pair WER evaluation; its 87% one-word switch recall and 1.6% loanword misrouting meet gate criteria.
Benchmark SwitchGate-320 against a 320-ms multilingual RNN-T on unseen Arabic–Spanish/Hindi–French pairs, measuring ±3-word switch WER and monolingual WER.
SwitchGate-320 benchmark report tabulates per-pair ±3-word switch WER, monolingual WER deltas, and latency against the matched RNN-T.
Ablate loanword negatives and backbone freezing on held-out Hindi–French switches and monolingual loanwords, measuring recall and misrouting.
Hindi–French ablation: frozen SwitchGate-320 achieved 83% one-word recall but raised monolingual WER 0.8 points versus matched RNN-T at 320-ms latency.
Train a shared phoneme-space transducer with sparse cross-lingual lexical biasing and a confidence-gated monolingual bypass at 320-ms latency.
Train a phoneme transducer with sparse biasing and monolingual bypass; compare unseen-pair switch-window and monolingual WER against 320-ms RNN-T.
Use the SwitchGate-320 report’s worst unseen pair to tune phoneme-bias sparsity and bypass thresholds on separate development utterances.
PhonoBias-320 configuration specifies top-8 lexical biasing and a 0.82 monolingual-bypass confidence threshold, with report-selected-pair development provenance.
Does PhonoBias-320’s 0.82 bypass threshold suppress lexical biasing near ambiguous switches in unseen language pairs?
At 0.82, the monolingual bypass suppresses top-8 lexical biasing on at least 20% of ambiguous unseen-pair switches.
Replay PhonoBias-320 on held-out Hindi–French ambiguous switches and monolingual clips; measure bypass suppression frequency, ±3-word WER, and monolingual WER.
On held-out Hindi–French, PhonoBias-320’s bypass suppressed lexical biasing on 27% of ambiguous switches, exceeding the 20% threshold.
Audit 0.82 bypass decisions on held-out Arabic–Spanish ambiguous switches against bypass-disabled decoding, recording suppression rate and ±3-word WER.
On held-out Arabic–Spanish, PhonoBias-320’s bypass suppressed biasing on only 9% of ambiguous switches, below the hypothesized 20%.
At 0.82, unseen pairs with switch-local bypass-confidence ECE >0.10 show >20% suppression; pairs with ECE <0.05 show <10%.
Test PhonoBias-320’s 0.82 bypass on four additional unseen pairings, recording per-pair ambiguous-switch suppression against the original 20% threshold.
Across four additional unseen pairings, PhonoBias-320 suppressed lexical biasing on 23–29% of ambiguous switches per pair at 0.82.
Measure switch-local ECE and suppression across six unseen pairings; test >20% suppression above 0.10 ECE, <10% below 0.05.
Across six unseen pairings, Arabic–Spanish had switch-local ECE 0.13 but only 9% suppression, contradicting the high-ECE prediction.
Compute signed calibration error and suppression by confidence bin for Arabic–Spanish and five other unseen pairs at the 0.82 threshold.
Five unseen pairs met n20’s high-ECE prediction (ECE 0.11–0.16; suppression 23–29%); Arabic–Spanish’s contrary error reflected underconfidence.
Replace unsigned ECE with signed overconfidence for bypass tuning: five pairs fit the prediction, but underconfident Arabic–Spanish suppressed only 9%.
Train a signed-overconfidence-aware bypass calibrator for PhonoBias-320 to protect unseen-pair switches and monolingual accuracy at 320-ms latency.
Can a pair-agnostic causal calibrator estimate signed switch-local overconfidence without labeled target-pair switches or increasing 320-ms latency?
A seen-pair-trained causal calibrator predicts switch-local overconfidence sign ≥80% accurately on unseen pairs without target-pair labels or exceeding 320-ms latency.
Fit a causal calibrator on seen-pair confidence traces; assess overconfidence-sign accuracy and streaming latency on six held-out pairings.
Benchmark the seen-pair-trained causal calibrator on six held-out pairings, scoring overconfidence-sign accuracy against reference switches and streaming latency.
Across six held-out pairings, the seen-pair-trained calibrator predicted switch-local overconfidence sign with 83% accuracy at 320-ms streaming latency.
Audit Arabic–Spanish underconfidence-sign accuracy using reference switches, verifying zero target-pair training examples and 320-ms streaming latency.
Arabic–Spanish switch audit found 61% sign accuracy and 390-ms p95 latency under burst traffic, exceeding the 320-ms limit.
A quantized acoustic-uncertainty calibrator achieves ≥80% sign accuracy per unseen pair and ≤320-ms p95 burst latency without target-pair labels.
Quantize the acoustic-uncertainty calibrator trained on seen pairs; test per-pair sign accuracy and p95 burst latency without target-pair training.
Run int8 acoustic-uncertainty calibration on six unseen pairs, auditing each pair’s sign accuracy and p95 latency under burst traffic.
Int8 acoustic calibration achieved 81–88% sign accuracy per unseen pair and 310-ms p95 burst latency without target-pair training.
Adopt int8 acoustic calibration: 81–88% per-pair sign accuracy, 310-ms p95; original’s 83% aggregate masked 61% Arabic–Spanish accuracy and 390-ms bursts.
Benchmark int8-calibrated PhonoBias-320 against matched-latency multilingual RNN-T on six unseen pairs, scoring ±3-word switch WER and monolingual WER deltas.
PhonoBias-320 benchmark report records six unseen-pair switch-window WER reductions, monolingual WER deltas, and matched-latency checks.
Train a boundary-specialist RNN-T on synthetic recombined-language switches with monolingual KL anchoring to the matched baseline at 320-ms latency.
Train boundary-specialist RNN-T with synthetic switches and monolingual KL anchoring; benchmark unseen-pair switch-window WER and monolingual WER at 320 ms.
Generate 200,000 synthetic switch utterances from disjoint monolingual corpora; train RNN-T with three-word boundary weighting and KL anchoring.
BoundaryRNN-T-320 checkpoint and training manifest include 200,000 synthetic switches, three-word boundary weighting, and monolingual KL anchoring.
Does BoundaryRNN-T-320 mistake monolingual loanwords for synthetic switch boundaries despite KL anchoring?
KL anchoring keeps loanword-adjacent monolingual WER within 0.5 points of the matched RNN-T while retaining ≥15% relative switch-window improvement.
Score BoundaryRNN-T-320 against matched RNN-T on held-out loanword-adjacent monolingual clips and six unseen-pair ±3-word switch windows at 320 ms.
At 320 ms, BoundaryRNN-T-320 cut switch-window WER 17–21% across six unseen pairs; loanword-adjacent monolingual WER rose 0.3 points.
Stress-test BoundaryRNN-T-320 on monolingual loanwords absent from synthetic-switch training, measuring loanword-adjacent WER against matched RNN-T.
On loanwords absent from training, BoundaryRNN-T-320 raised adjacent monolingual WER 0.9 points over matched RNN-T at 320 ms.
Monolingual loanword negatives plus KL anchoring keep unseen-loanword-adjacent WER degradation below 0.5 points while preserving ≥15% unseen-pair switch-window gains.
Add held-out-lexicon loanword negatives during boundary training, then remeasure unseen-loanword monolingual WER and unseen-pair switch-window WER.
Retrain BoundaryRNN-T-320 with disjoint loanword negatives; compare reserved-loanword WER and six unseen-pair switch-window WER at 320 ms.
With loanword negatives, reserved-loanword WER rose 0.4 points; unseen-pair switch-window WER fell 16–19% versus matched RNN-T.
Audit loanword-negative model on rare, unseen loanwords and held-out Turkish–Japanese switches, comparing both WER metrics at 320 ms.
At 320 ms, loanword-negative BoundaryRNN-T-320 raised rare-loanword WER 0.7 points and reduced Turkish–Japanese switch-window WER only 12% versus baseline.
Do not advance BoundaryRNN-T-320: six pairs passed, but rare-loanword WER rose 0.7 points and Turkish–Japanese improved only 12%.
Following BoundaryRNN-T-320’s rejection, phonetic-hard negatives and script-balanced synthesis with KL anchoring yield <0.5-point rare-loanword degradation and ≥15% Turkish–Japanese gains.
Train with phonetically confusable loanword negatives and script-balanced switches; test rare-loanword and Turkish–Japanese WER against the matched baseline.
Train KL-anchored BoundaryRNN-T-320 with phonetic-hard negatives and script-balanced switches; measure rare-loanword degradation and unseen-pair switch-window gains at 320 ms.
With phonetic-hard negatives, rare-loanword WER rose 0.3 points; seven unseen pairs, including Turkish–Japanese, showed 16–19% lower switch-window WER versus baseline.
Ablate script-balanced synthesis and phonetic-hard negatives separately on Turkish–Japanese switches and rare loanwords, measuring WER against baseline at 320 ms.
On rare homophone loanwords, combined training raised WER 0.6 points versus baseline; removing script balancing limited degradation to 0.4.
Keep BoundaryRNN-T-320 deferred: seven-pair switch gains improved, but 0.6-point homophone degradation breaches the monolingual limit.
Audit deferred BoundaryRNN-T-320’s rare-homophone errors: compare boundary posteriors on loanwords across script-balanced and unbalanced checkpoints at 320 ms.
Rare-homophone audit lists loanword-level boundary posteriors, recognition errors, and script-balanced versus unbalanced checkpoint differences at 320 ms.
Train a 320-ms articulatory-unit RNN-T with language-span dropout to discourage pair memorization and monolingual teacher distillation to preserve accuracy.
Does language-span dropout improve unseen-pair switch recognition without corrupting articulatory-unit decoding on monolingual rare homophones?
With 20% span dropout and teacher distillation, articulatory RNN-T achieves ≥15% unseen-pair switch-window WER reduction and <0.5-point rare-homophone degradation.
Train ArticRNN-T-320 with 20% span dropout and distillation; assess unseen-pair switch-window and monolingual rare-homophone WER at matched latency.
Compare ArticRNN-T-320 with PhonoBias-320’s report on six unseen pairs; score switch-window and rare-homophone WER against baseline at 320 ms.
On PhonoBias-320’s six unseen pairs, ArticRNN-T-320 cut switch-window WER 16–20% versus baseline; rare-homophone WER rose 0.3 points at 320 ms.
Reproduce PhonoBias-320 report’s six-pair baseline comparisons with ArticRNN-T-320; separately test Turkish–Japanese switch and out-of-lexicon homophone WER at 320 ms.
On Turkish–Japanese, ArticRNN-T-320 cut switch-window WER only 11% versus baseline; out-of-lexicon homophone WER rose 0.7 points at 320 ms.
Script-stratified language-span dropout plus rare-homophone contrastive distillation yields ≥15% Turkish–Japanese switch-window WER reduction and <0.5-point out-of-lexicon homophone degradation.
Stratify dropout by script, add rare-homophone contrastive distillation, then retest Turkish–Japanese switch-window and out-of-lexicon homophone WER.
Benchmark script-stratified ArticRNN-T-320 with contrastive distillation against PhonoBias-320’s six-pair report; score Turkish–Japanese switch-window and out-of-lexicon homophone WER.
At 320 ms, script-stratified ArticRNN-T-320 reduced Turkish–Japanese switch-window WER 17% versus baseline; out-of-lexicon homophone WER rose 0.3 points.
Replay audited rare-homophone errors and Turkish–Japanese switches through script-stratified ArticRNN-T-320; compare boundary posteriors and WER against baseline.
On audited rare homophones, ArticRNN-T-320 reduced false boundary activations 31% versus BoundaryRNN-T-320; monolingual WER rose 0.4 points versus baseline.
Advance revised ArticRNN-T-320 for six-pair retesting: Turkish–Japanese improved from 11% to 17%, and audited homophone degradation stayed within 0.4 points.
Retest revised ArticRNN-T-320 against matched RNN-T on six unseen pairs and monolingual homophones, measuring ±3-word WER, monolingual WER, and latency.
Revised ArticRNN-T-320 retest report tabulates six unseen-pair ±3-word WER reductions, monolingual homophone WER deltas, and matched-latency results.

requirements: Reduce WER within three words of switches by 15% relative to a matched multilingual baseline.
Evaluate unseen pairings; keep monolingual WER degradation below 0.5 percentage points at matched streaming latency.
